title: Will farm animals always suffer? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Factory farming follows an income-driven industrialization curve, and a handful of rich countries (Germany, Sweden, New Zealand) are now showing the first signs of a Kuznets-style bend toward less total animal suffering, driven mainly by cheap welfare technology rather than falling meat demand, while alternative proteins remain too expensive to matter yet.

themes.theme: Scale and drivers of industrial factory farming

insights.claim: A 26-storey pig farm opened in Ezhou, China in September 2022, with a second tower following months later, and together these high-rises raise more than a million pigs a year that never go outside.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates how far vertical integration and automation in meat production has gone in China, a template that could scale to other high-income-growth countries.
insights.quote: More than a million pigs are born, raised, and slaughtered each year without ever setting foot outside.
insights.locator: In September 2022, a new kind of pig farm opened in China

insights.claim: Farming industrializes on a predictable income schedule: chicken farming starts to industrialize once average income reaches about $1,000, battery cages dominate egg production by $10,000, and almost all pigs are raised in warehouses above $30,000 average income.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Gives investors a rough income threshold model to forecast which emerging markets are about to see industrial-scale meat production build-out.
insights.quote: Once average incomes reach around $1,000, chicken farming starts to industrialize.
insights.locator: As countries get wealthier, farming consolidates

insights.claim: Industrially farmed animals suffer significant harms: chickens have their beaks sheared off and legs too weak to support their bloated bodies, pigs have tails docked and teeth clipped without anesthesia, and mother pigs spend much of their lives in gestation crates too small to turn around in.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Defines the specific welfare harms that regulation, retailer standards, and welfare-labeled product lines target.
insights.quote: Chickens’ beaks are frequently sheared off and their legs are too weak to support their bloated bodies.
insights.locator: But industrially farmed animals suffer immensely for it

insights.claim: South Korea's meat supply per person rose fivefold during Park Chung Hee's rule from 1961 to 1979, and tenfold by 2000, from a 1961 baseline of around four kilograms per person per year.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows how fast meat demand can scale during an income takeoff, a pattern relevant to forecasting protein demand in current fast-growing emerging economies.
insights.quote: When Park Chung Hee took power in 1961, South Korea’s meat supply was around four kilograms per person per year, less than the weight of two chickens.
insights.locator: When Park Chung Hee took power in 1961

insights.claim: Rising meat consumption in industrializing countries has coincided with major human physical development gains, with average South Korean male height rising from about 160cm in 1961 to about 175cm today, and Chinese men gaining a similar amount.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Complicates simple anti-meat policy narratives, since rising meat consumption in poor countries is tied to real nutrition and health gains, not just taste preference.
insights.quote: In South Korea, average male height has increased from around 160 centimeters in 1961 (five feet three inches) to around 175 centimeters (five feet nine inches) today.
insights.locator: In poor countries, where inadequate nutrition is the norm

themes.theme: The Kuznets curve as a framework for animal suffering

insights.claim: The Kuznets curve concept, originally describing how economic inequality rises then falls with national wealth, has been applied to many other trajectories including air pollution, deforestation, and obesity, which worsen during industrialization but improve once countries pass a wealth threshold.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Provides the core analytical lens the article uses to assess whether animal welfare will self-correct with rising wealth, useful for framing any similar ESG or externality thesis.
insights.quote: Simon Kuznets, who suggested that economic inequality rose as countries first industrialized but then fell as they became even richer.
insights.locator: These trajectories are called Kuznets curves

insights.claim: London's air pollution, vividly described by Dickens in 1853, kept worsening for nearly another half-century, then halved within a hundred years and was less than a tenth as dirty by 2000.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Serves as the article's benchmark case for how long a Kuznets-style reversal can take once it starts.
insights.quote: flakes of soot … as big as full-grown snowflakes
insights.locator: In his 1853 masterpiece Bleak House

insights.claim: Global forest loss peaked in 1980 and typically reverses once a country's average income reaches between $5,000 and $15,000, as improved crop yields make farming more land-efficient and marginal farmland reverts to nature.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Establishes an income-threshold precedent analogous to the animal-welfare threshold the article later identifies.
insights.quote: forest loss typically reverses when average incomes enter the range between $5,000 and $15,000, as farming becomes more efficient and marginal farmland reverts to nature.
insights.locator: Growing economies and populations have historically driven deforestation

insights.claim: Kuznets curves fail to bend when the costs of industrial activity are not borne locally by the rich country: carbon emissions have fallen sharply in Germany and Britain but far less in the United States and Australia, and total material consumption and waste generation keep growing worldwide rather than declining.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Flags the key risk to any thesis that animal welfare automatically improves with wealth: it depends on whether the harm is locally visible and costly, which is uncertain for animal suffering.
insights.quote: Emissions have fallen substantially in Germany and Britain, but much less in America and Australia, which remain some of the world’s biggest carbon emitters.
insights.locator: But Kuznets curves don’t appear in all places

themes.theme: Diverging meat consumption trends in rich countries

insights.claim: Meat consumption per capita appears to have peaked in about ten European countries, including Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, and Denmark, with people now eating markedly less than they did in the early 2000s.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Identifies a small cluster of markets where meat-industry volume growth has genuinely reversed, relevant for European protein and food-retail investors.
insights.quote: In about ten European countries, including Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, and Denmark, meat consumption per capita appears to have peaked.
insights.locator: How much meat do we eat?

insights.claim: German pork consumption fell more than 10 percent in the five years before 2025, with supermarket shelf space shifting toward marinated chicken, ready meals, and plant-based sausages, and 34 university cafeterias across Berlin moving to menus that were 96 percent plant-based by 2021.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of institutional and retail-level demand shift that plant-based food companies could point to as a real, not just survey-based, market signal in Germany.
insights.quote: Pork, once the unquestioned centerpiece of German cuisine, has lost its grip: consumption fell over 10 percent just in the five years before 2025.
insights.locator: Walk into a German supermarket today

insights.claim: In most rich countries, including Portugal, Spain, the United States, Britain, South Korea, and Australia, meat consumption is not declining but plateauing at roughly 150 kilograms per person per year, suggesting an upper demand ceiling rather than continued unbounded growth.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic demand ceiling of ~150kg/person/year for protein producers and food companies modeling long-run volume growth in mature meat markets.
insights.quote: have all reached a ceiling of around 150 kilograms of meat per person per year.
insights.locator: But many rich countries aren’t like Germany or Denmark

insights.claim: New high-protein dietary guidance recommending two grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily could, if half met with meat, require the average American to double meat consumption, while GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic appear to shift users toward protein-rich foods even as they reduce total caloric intake.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Flags protein-fad dieting and anti-obesity drug adoption as swing factors that could push meat demand above its current plateau, worth monitoring for protein and alt-protein investors.
insights.quote: Drugs like Ozempic suppress appetite and reduce total caloric intake, but evidence suggests users shift toward protein-rich foods to preserve muscles
insights.locator: Whether this ceiling holds may depend on shifting dietary fashions

insights.claim: Even though Germans ate about a fifth less meat by weight in 2022 than in 1980, the number of animals slaughtered to supply the average German diet doubled from about ten to twenty per year, driven by a shift from beef toward chicken (about 14 per year) and farmed fish (about six per year).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows that falling meat volume does not equal falling animal suffering once species mix shifts toward smaller animals, a key nuance for any animal-welfare-linked investment or ESG screen.
insights.quote: that number had doubled to twenty animals, largely driven by the shift to chicken and farmed fish
insights.locator: In 1980, the average German diet required the slaughter of about ten farmed animals per year

insights.claim: Species mix matters more than volume for total welfare: beef implies roughly a day or two of suffering per kilogram, chicken implies dozens of days of suffering per kilogram, and farmed fish implies hundreds to thousands of days of suffering per kilogram depending on the species.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Suggests animal-welfare-focused investors and ESG screens should weight species composition of a company's supply chain far more heavily than total meat volume or calories.
insights.quote: Beef implies perhaps a day or two of suffering per kilogram, whereas chicken implies dozens of days of suffering per kilogram and farmed fish hundreds or thousands, depending on the species.
insights.locator: From a welfare perspective, that makes a tremendous difference

themes.theme: Cheap technology, not falling demand, is driving welfare reform

insights.claim: Decades of industry focus on cost efficiency have made meat historically cheap: in 1946 an average American factory worker needed more than half an hour of wages to buy a pound of chicken, versus about four minutes today, leaving room for cheap welfare upgrades without large price impacts.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains why welfare reforms have been commercially adoptable: the cost base is so low that small welfare-driven cost increases are easily absorbed by consumers.
insights.quote: In 1946, the average American factory worker had to work more than half an hour to buy a pound of chicken. Today it takes four minutes.
insights.locator: For decades, the animal agriculture industry has focused on efficiency

insights.claim: Cage-free egg adoption has scaled rapidly in wealthy markets, now covering 45 percent of American, 62 percent of European, and 82 percent of British hens, sparing hundreds of millions of hens annually at a marginal cost of only one to two cents more per egg.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cage-free conversion is a proven, low-cost welfare intervention with strong adoption data, useful as a benchmark for evaluating other welfare-tech rollouts.
insights.quote: Today, 45 percent of American, 62 percent of European, and 82 percent of British hens are kept in cage-free facilities.
insights.locator: In wealthy countries, consumers and companies have shifted

insights.claim: Battery cage bans have come through direct ballot referenda with resounding majorities in Switzerland, Massachusetts, and California, while in Sweden retailers and shoppers eliminated caged eggs without any legislation, leaving almost all Swedish hens cage-free by 2025.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows welfare reform can be driven by either direct democracy or pure market/retailer pressure, two distinct policy and consumer-pressure pathways to watch in other markets.
insights.quote: By 2025, almost all hens in Sweden were cage-free thanks to retailers and shoppers rejecting caged eggs.
insights.locator: In some countries and regions, cages for hens have been eradicated at the ballot box

insights.claim: The EU and US now require cattle and pigs to be stunned before slaughter (with religious-slaughter exemptions), and gestation-crate and baby-cow-crate bans have spread across the EU, New Zealand, and several US states since the 2000s, alongside restrictions on unanesthetized tail docking and castration in the EU and Britain.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Maps the current regulatory frontier for animal welfare that companies selling into these markets must already comply with.
insights.quote: Crates that confine pregnant sows and baby cows to spaces too small to turn around in have gradually been banned across the European Union, New Zealand, and several US states since the 2000s.
insights.locator: Other practices in husbandry are following a similar path

insights.claim: In ovo sexing technology, which identifies chick sex at the embryo stage so male eggs can be discarded before hatching, has already spared hundreds of millions of male chicks in Europe from being gassed or ground up on their first day of life, and has only just begun spreading in the US.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term technology adoption opportunity in the US market for animal-welfare-tech investors, given proven Europe-scale deployment.
insights.quote: In ovo sexing allows farmers to figure out the sex of chicks at the embryo stage, discarding eggs containing males.
insights.locator: New technologies can reduce suffering even further

insights.claim: New Zealand is the clearest current example of a country plausibly reducing total farm animal suffering, having banned battery cages, restricted sow crates, and mandated pre-slaughter stunning while also eating less meat, with Germany and Sweden potentially following a similar combined path.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Identifies the only country-level case studies where the animal-suffering Kuznets curve may already be bending, useful benchmarks for tracking whether other wealthy markets follow.
insights.quote: New Zealand has banned battery cages, restricted sow crates, and mandated pre-slaughter stunning, and is also eating far less meat.
insights.locator: But in a few countries, the combination of declining meat eating and improved treatment

themes.theme: What it takes to bend the curve, and the limits of alternative proteins

insights.claim: Belief that farm animals suffer and that their welfare matters is nearly universal across income levels, with 70 to 90 percent agreement whether surveyed in Sudan or Singapore, but willingness to pay for higher-welfare products rises sharply with wealth, from 42 percent of Europe's poorest income quintile to 72 percent of the richest.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Defines a wealth-segmented addressable market for premium welfare-labeled animal products: target the top income quintiles first, since concern for welfare doesn't translate to willingness to pay until income rises.
insights.quote: In European surveys, 42 percent of the poorest quintile say they would pay more for higher-welfare products. Among the richest quintile, it’s 72 percent.
insights.locator: Income needs to reach a certain level before things can start to change

insights.claim: No poor country has bent the animal-suffering curve, and the countries showing progress are all high-income (New Zealand at $45,000, Germany at $55,000, Denmark at $65,000 average income), but income alone is insufficient since Japan, South Korea, and the United States have surpassed these thresholds yet still show rising meat consumption and weaker welfare reform than peers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Warns against a simple income-threshold investment thesis for animal-welfare reform; large wealthy economies like Japan, South Korea, and the US are lagging counterexamples.
insights.quote: New Zealand has an average income of $45,000, Germany $55,000, and Denmark $65,000.
insights.locator: No poor country has bent the curve

insights.claim: Animal welfare improves fastest where the enabling technology is already cheap, as with stunning machines and cage-free housing, while plant-based and cultivated meat have made almost no dent in animal suffering, together holding less than 2 percent of overall meat market share, largely because of cost.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Signals that alt-protein investment theses hinge almost entirely on reaching cost parity with conventional meat, not on consumer demand or awareness, which are already high.
insights.quote: the entire alternative meat industry has yet to reach more than 2 percent market share for meat overall
insights.locator: Animal welfare improves fastest when the technology is already cheaply available

insights.claim: The only cultivated meat currently sold in supermarkets is a Singaporean company's shredded chicken product that is just 3 percent cultivated chicken cells and 97 percent plant-based, yet still retails at more than $20 per pound, roughly ten times the price of conventional chicken and about five times the price of pasture-raised chicken.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how far cultivated meat remains from cost parity, implying investors should not expect near-term market-share gains without an order-of-magnitude cost reduction.
insights.quote: a shredded chicken product that is 3 percent cultivated chicken cells and 97 percent plant-based, and retails at more than twenty dollars per pound
insights.locator: The only cultivated meat currently sold in supermarkets

insights.claim: Historical Kuznets-style reversals suggest bending the animal-suffering curve could take decades even after the problem is well understood: leaded gasoline poisoned children for most of the twentieth century until blood lead levels plummeted within a decade of 1970s phase-outs, and London's air pollution worsened for two centuries before its decline, meaning a workable low-cost substitute has to exist alongside public awareness before the curve bends.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic multi-decade timeline for animal-welfare-linked investment theses (alt protein, welfare-certified supply chains) rather than expecting a near-term inflection point.
insights.quote: For most of the twentieth century, leaded gasoline poisoned children’s blood across the developed world until lead levels plummeted within a decade of countries phasing it out in the 1970s.
insights.locator: Those curves began to bend when the problem became undeniable
